description: Width tiers for Year 10 Science — ACARA v9. Covers the seven U-strand descriptors. H-strand and I-strand (9–10 band) are in science_y9_10_width_tiers.json.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor grounded in the most common elaboration cases.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding phenomena, cultural contexts or applications. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations treated as source data. Typical grounded in common cases; wider may infer within the descriptor's territory and year band.

AC9S10U01.minimum_width: Describe the DNA-gene-chromosome hierarchy; explain how meiosis produces varied gametes; complete a Punnett square for a monohybrid cross and predict the phenotype ratio.
AC9S10U01.typical_width: Explain chromosome-DNA-gene hierarchy using models; describe meiosis producing varied gametes (halving chromosome number, independent assortment, crossing over); explain fertilisation restoring diploid number; predict genotype and phenotype ratios for dominant/recessive and sex-linked crosses; use pedigree diagrams to trace inheritance patterns.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' knowledge of heredity encoded in kinship systems and marriage laws
Explore environmental and other factors that cause mutations and identify changes in DNA or chromosomes
Examine applications of gene technologies (gene therapy, genetic engineering) and biotechnologies producing therapeutic proteins (AC9S10H02)
Use pedigree diagrams to trace patterns of inheritance through multigenerational families for dominant and recessive characteristics
elaborations: using models and diagrams to represent the relationship between genes, chromosomes, and DNA
explaining how genetic information passed on to offspring from both parents by meiosis and fertilisation increases variation
using Mendelian inheritance to predict offspring genotypes and phenotypes in monohybrid crosses
using pedigree diagrams to show patterns of inheritance through multigenerational families
investigating First Nations Australians' knowledges of heredity as evidenced by kinship and family structures
exploring environmental and other factors that cause mutations

AC9S10U02.minimum_width: Explain the four steps of natural selection; apply natural selection to a named population under a specific selection pressure; describe at least three lines of evidence for evolution.
AC9S10U02.typical_width: Explain natural selection (variation, selection pressure, differential reproduction, population change); apply to artificial selection; connect genetic characteristics to survival and reproduction rates; analyse fossil record, homologous structures, DNA similarities and geographical distribution as independent evidence lines; explain how multiple independent lines converge to strengthen the theory.
wider: Investigate structural and physiological adaptations of First Nations Australians to the Australian environment — examining long-term natural selection in human populations
Examine biodiversity as a function of evolution from common ancestors — explaining divergence through natural selection
Explore how DNA sequencing added powerful molecular evidence to anatomical and fossil evidence — connecting technology to evidence strengthening (AC9S10H02)
Investigate changes caused by natural selection in a specific population under a specified selection pressure — examining a documented rapid evolution case
elaborations: outlining processes involved in natural selection including variation, isolation and selection
examining biodiversity as a function of evolution
analysing evidence for the theory of evolution including fossil record, chemical and anatomical similarities, and geographical distribution
investigating changes caused by natural selection in a population under a specified selection pressure
relating genetic characteristics to survival and reproductive rates
investigating some structural and physiological adaptations of First Nations Australians to the Australian environment

AC9S10U03.minimum_width: Describe the big bang theory; construct or annotate a timeline of at least four major stages of universe evolution; describe at least three lines of evidence for the big bang and explain what each contributes.
AC9S10U03.typical_width: Describe the big bang model; construct a universe evolution timeline using appropriate units (light-years, scientific notation); describe major universe components; explain how stellar spectra reveal composition, movement and distance; examine CMB radiation, red/blue shift, Hubble's observations and matter proportions as converging evidence; explain how gravitational wave detection validated general relativity.
wider: Research First Nations Australians' knowledges of celestial bodies and cosmological explanations — comparing with the big bang model as different knowledge frameworks
Explore recent advances: gravitational waves, dark matter, dark energy discoveries and how these refined understanding (AC9S10H02)
Examine how the Australian SKA Pathfinder enables unprecedented data collection — connecting technology to knowledge advance
Examine why gravitational wave discovery didn't occur until 100 years after Einstein's prediction — connecting technology readiness to validation timing (AC9S10H01)
elaborations: describing the major components of the universe using appropriate scientific terminology including light-years
constructing a timeline of major changes from Big Bang to formation of stars and galaxies
examining how stars' light spectra reveal composition, movement and distance
explaining how cosmic microwave background radiation, red/blue shift, Hubble's observations and matter proportions support the big bang
researching First Nations Australians' knowledges of celestial bodies and explanations of the origin of the universe
identifying technologies used to collect astronomical data
exploring recent advances including SKA Pathfinder and discovery of gravitational waves, dark matter and dark energy

AC9S10U04.minimum_width: Explain the role of solar radiation in driving global climate; describe how greenhouse gas increases alter Earth's energy balance; describe at least four climate change indicators.
AC9S10U04.typical_width: Explain how solar radiation drives atmospheric and ocean circulation; describe greenhouse effect and amplification from increased CO₂; describe ocean current roles in climate regulation; examine ocean/atmospheric temperature, sea level, biodiversity, species distribution, permafrost and sea ice as indicators; use visualisations and simulations to explore energy balance changes; evaluate mitigation strategies.
wider: Investigate how satellite data generates global measurements of ocean temperatures, sea levels and ice cover (AC9S10H02)
Examine how traditional ecological knowledges of First Nations Australians are being reaffirmed by climate science and applied in carbon farming (AC9S10H03)
Explore how quantum computers enhance modelling of complex weather and climate systems (AC9S10H02)
Analyse data from multiple indicators to construct an argument about the direction and pace of climate change (AC9S10I07)
elaborations: examining the role of radiation from the sun and how its interactions with atmosphere, ocean and land are the foundation for the global climate system
investigating indicators of climate change such as changes in ocean and atmospheric temperatures, sea levels, biodiversity, species distribution, permafrost and sea ice
identifying changes in global climate over time and exploring visualisations and simulations
examining the factors that drive deep ocean currents and their role in regulating global climate
investigating how quantum computers enhance modelling of complex weather and climate systems
predicting changes to the Earth system and identifying strategies to reduce or mitigate climate change

AC9S10U05.minimum_width: State Newton's three laws and apply each to a named context; use F=ma to solve for one unknown; interpret a distance-time and a speed-time graph.
AC9S10U05.typical_width: Apply Newton's three laws to diverse motion contexts; use F=ma quantitatively; analyse distance, speed and acceleration relationships graphically; model how changed net force affects motion; evaluate vehicle safety features (seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones) using force-time reasoning.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians achieve increased speed and impact force through spearthrowers and bows — examining Newton's laws applied to traditional technologies
Investigate Newton's laws applications in sport — examining how these improve athlete performance or safety
Investigate how driverless vehicles apply Newton's laws to brake in time
Construct a data-supported argument for lower speed limits near schools or for urban trucks (AC9S10I07)
elaborations: investigating a moving object to analyse relationships between distance, time, speed, force and acceleration
using mathematical representations to quantitatively relate force, speed, acceleration and mass
investigating how First Nations Australians achieve increased speed and impact force through spearthrowers and bows
modelling how change in net force affects motion and relating to safety features
investigating Newton's laws applications in sport
constructing a data-supported argument for lower speed limits
investigating how driverless vehicles apply Newton's laws to brake in time

AC9S10U06.minimum_width: Draw Bohr models for at least three elements and identify their group from outer electron count; explain why same-group elements have similar properties; identify at least two periodic table patterns.
AC9S10U06.typical_width: Use the Bohr model to describe electron shell structure for elements across periods; explain how outer electron number determines reactivity and bonding; identify group patterns (similar properties) and period trends (progressive shell filling); deduce that periodic patterns reflect outer electron shell patterns; investigate physical properties of metals and non-metals.
wider: Conduct flame tests for selected elements and examine emission spectra — connecting spectral evidence to the Bohr model of discrete electron energy levels
Examine how the spectroscope's development led to refinement of the atomic model (AC9S10H01, AC9S9U06)
Analyse periodic table patterns to predict properties of elements based on position — using the table predictively
Compare merits and limitations of periodic table representation vs graphical representations of patterns such as melting point
elaborations: examining how elements are organised in the periodic table and analysing patterns
investigating physical properties of some metals and non-metals
using the Bohr model to describe atom structure in terms of electron shells
deducing that repeating periodic patterns reflect outer electron shell patterns
conducting flame tests and examining emission spectra
examining how the spectroscope led to further development of the atomic model

AC9S10U07.minimum_width: Define synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions; write or identify a balanced equation for each type; explain how at least three factors affect reaction rate with particle-level reasoning.
AC9S10U07.typical_width: Define and represent all three reaction types using molecular models, word and balanced equations; identify reaction type and predict products; investigate synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions; investigate how temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts affect rate; represent rate data graphically.
wider: Investigate chemical reactions First Nations Australians use in producing substances such as acids and ethanol
Investigate First Nations Australians' methods for converting toxic plants into edible food products — examining the chemistry underlying traditional food processing
Examine reactions used to extract metals and identify the reaction type and rate considerations involved
Predict how green chemistry principles will affect industrial chemistry practice — connecting rate and reaction type knowledge to sustainability
elaborations: defining and representing synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions
identifying reaction type and predicting products
investigating synthesis, decomposition and displacement reactions across multiple examples
investigating the effect of temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts on reaction rates
investigating chemical reactions employed by First Nations Australians in producing substances such as acids and ethanol
investigating First Nations Australians' methods to convert toxic plants into edible food
examining reactions that produce useful products
